_readme: Main Salmon camp guide data — the source for web/main-salmon-camps.html.
Build: node scripts/build-camp-guide.mjs main-salmon
m/n/s/lo/hi/r/fs come straight from the Forest Service list and are the
authority: 'Wild Main Salmon Campsites' (2025 Camp List for Website.pdf,
Salmon-Challis NF, https://www.fs.usda.gov/media/233548), read 2026-09-30.
m   river mile          s   river side (L/R, looking downstream)
lo  low-water capacity  hi  high-water capacity (0 = no camp at that level)
r   'L' large reservable, 'S' small-medium reservable, null first-come
fs  the Forest Service remark, verbatim
d (and lowNote/highNote) are LateBoof's own words. Anything in them beyond
the Forest Service remark is corroborated by GoRafting's mile-by-mile Main
Salmon guide (https://gorafting.com/united-states/idaho/main-salmon/), read
the same day; src lists which sources an entry leans on ('fs', 'gr').
Where the two disagree the Forest Service wins and `conflict` says so.
Nothing here is from a LateBoof trip yet — do not add detail without a source.
t = attribute tags (see TAGS in the build script). photos = optional
{ low: {src, alt, credit}, high: {...} }; src is a base name under
web/img/camps/main-salmon/ with -720.webp and -1200.webp variants.
landmarks = non-camp labels on the strip map (web/camp-rail.js): the put-in,
the end of the Wild section (Forest Service list) and the two ramps (GoRafting
miles; Carey Creek is 81.0 there and sits at the end of the mapped line).
gauge = reference gauge for the aerial captions. anchors = creek mouths whose Forest
Service mile pins the map line and the aerials (see build-camp-aerials.mjs).

fs.label: Forest Service, Wild Main Salmon Campsites (2025)

fsRules.label: Salmon-Challis National Forest, Wild Main Salmon River

gr.label: GoRafting, Main Salmon River Rafting Guide

sections.title: Corn Creek to Black Canyon
sections.blurb: The first day or two. Short mileage between camps, the Lantz Bar and Devil's Teeth clusters, and the first reservable sites.

sections.title: Black Canyon to Big Mallard
sections.blurb: Black Creek Rapid, the Barth hot springs camps, then a quieter stretch down to Bargamin Creek and the Yellowpine and Mallard camps.

sections.title: Big Mallard to the South Fork
sections.blurb: Homestead country: Jim Moore's place, Campbell's Ferry, Buckskin Bill's at Five Mile Bar, and the airstrips and pack bridge around Mackay Bar.

sections.title: South Fork to Long Tom Bar
sections.blurb: Below the South Fork the river is bigger and the canyon hotter. Mostly sand beaches, most of them low-water camps, and the last reservable sites before the take-outs.

camps.d: A small sloping sand beach that loses the sun early. Better known as a first-day lunch stop than a camp, but it works for a small group that launched late.
camps.lowNote: The beach gets bigger as the river drops.

camps.d: Upstream of Horse Creek, with the camp back in the trees rather than on a beach. Room for a full-size group at any level, and the closest big camp to the put-in.
On the bar just below the creek. Across the river are the remains of a pack bridge that was condemned and removed in 1970. The eddy is small, so set up for it early.
camps.lowNote: The bar is at its best at low water.

camps.d: A mid-sized sand beach on the left at Horse Creek, on the old pack bridge's side of the river. A low-water camp only.
An easy landing on a small beach, with the camp up by the trail. The Legend Creek pictographs are about 500 yards back upstream on foot. Watch for poison ivy.
A sloped beach leads up to tent sites on the bench beside the trail. Stone ruins left by 1950s settlers are nearby on the same bench. Small groups only.
Two sand beaches split by a band of rock, the upper one the bigger of the two, just above Rainier Rapid.
camps.lowNote: The beach keeps growing as the water drops.

camps.d: The first reservable camp on the river: a big, comfortable sand beach on the left bank across from Alder Creek. A natural first night for a large group once the water is down.
A small shaded beach at the bottom of a slow-water stretch. Low water only, and small groups only.
A shaded camp up on the bench, so it holds the same number of people at any water level.
The upstream camp at Lantz Bar. The eddy is large, but the Forest Service warns the camp is hard to see from the river, so know where it is before you get there.
A camp among the trees on the bench. The landing is a rocky bar upstream of the creek.
camps.highNote: The Forest Service calls this a high-water camp, and the rocky landing is easier with more water over it.

camps.d: A large bar above a sand beach, immediately above Lantz Rapid. The camp is on the bench, so it stays usable when the beach floods.
On the left immediately below Lantz Rapid, in the trees. A comfortable camp once you are up there.
camps.lowNote: The climb from the boats is rocky when the river is low.
camps.highNote: One of the dependable high-water camps in this stretch.

camps.d: A small low-water beach on the right below Lantz Rapid, across from Tag Creek.
A high bench downstream of the creek, reached by a trail from the river. Holds a big group at any level, but it is a hard carry in summer heat.
A pebble bar on the right just above Devil's Teeth Rapid. Groups float past it regularly. If you have it reserved, be on the right and looking for it before the rapid.
A large, pleasant camp on a high sandy bench below the rapid, good at any level. A pictograph panel is a short scramble downstream.
A small sand beach under the rock overhang that names it, visible from well upstream. Some boaters call it Hangover.
A large, good-looking camp up on the bar. The bank where you tie up is rocky.
A small low-water beach. Catch the eddy just above the creek. A trail on the downstream side of the creek climbs toward Chamberlain Basin.
A medium low-water beach, a step up in size from the 10-person beaches around it.
A shaded sand beach with the camp on a high bench in a ponderosa grove. Named for Dr. Walt Blackadar of Salmon, known for a solo descent of the Alsek in 1971. A full-size camp at any water level.
A sand beach just above a right-hand bend, with an old engine sitting in the middle of camp. The eddy is small.
camps.highNote: Mostly a low-water camp: the Forest Service cuts it from 30 people to 10 at high water.

camps.d: A sand beach with tent sites up on the bar, about a quarter mile below the creek and around the bend. This was the site of the Guth cabins.
camps.highNote: Drops from 20 people to 10 at high water.

camps.d: A large, rocky camp, partly shaded, that burned in 2000. Land at the upstream end of the bar before the river starts bending left. It sits well apart from the lower camp.
camps.highNote: A dependable high-water camp for a big group.

camps.d: A beach at the lower end of Corey Bar with a difficult approach.
camps.lowNote: The beach comes out as the river drops.
camps.highNote: No camp at high water, and the landing is fast if you try.

camps.d: A small low-water beach on the left, the last camp above Black Canyon. Not to be confused with the larger Pebble Beach at mile 53.2.
A small beach with an easy landing and a view back upstream into Black Canyon. It is the first camp below Black Creek Rapid, the Class IV that formed in a 2011 debris flow.
A rocky landing and a medium carry up to a shaded ponderosa grove on the bench. It is across the river from the Barth hot springs.
camps.lowNote: At low water you may still be able to get across to the hot springs from here.

camps.d: The first-come camp on the hot springs side of the river. A steep trail climbs from the boats to the bench. The springs themselves are closed to camping.
The reservable camp around the corner from Barth Hot Springs, and a good one. The price is the landing: strong current and rocks. Boatmen's inscriptions are carved in the rocks near the springs.
camps.lowNote: Look for the carved names and dates on the rocks when the river is low.

camps.d: A small beach below a high bench. Often used as the lunch stop after a soak at the hot springs.
A big camp reached by a high, rocky approach, downstream of Nixon Creek and on the opposite bank.
camps.highNote: A good high-water camp for a full-size group.

camps.d: A large and well-regarded camp behind a rocky approach.
camps.highNote: The Forest Service gives it no high-water capacity, and the landing gets hard as flows rise. On an early-season trip, stop upstream and look before you commit.

camps.d: A beach in the eddy immediately below Hancock Rapid. Start working left early in the rapid or you will be past it.
A large beach and long a popular camp. It burned in a 2023 wildfire, so expect less shade than older trip reports describe.
A small low-water camp with tent sites among the boulders and on the beach. The creek flash-flooded in 2024, so expect it to look different from older descriptions.
A big camp on a high bench about 50 yards below Bargamin Creek, good at any level. A good trail runs up the creek, and it is an easy walk downstream to scout Bailey Rapid.
camps.lowNote: A small beach appears below the bench.

camps.d: A nice sand beach below Bailey Rapid. Also a popular lunch stop, so expect company at midday.
A sand beach with a lot of poison ivy. The land above the beach is private, so stay on the sand.
A large beach below the Allison Ranch, a private inholding with its own airstrip. The ranch jet boat is often parked here.
camps.highNote: Shrinks from 30 people to 10 at high water.

camps.d: A nice big camp with a carry up from the sand. A good trail leads downstream to a view of Big Mallard Rapid, and wire from the Forest Service's old crank telephone line is still strung through camp.
A sand beach just below Upper Yellowpine and just above Big Mallard Rapid. The Forest Service remark calls it a low-water beach but keeps the capacity at 30 for both levels.
A large camp immediately below Big Mallard Rapid and Mallard Creek, good at any level. You run the rapid to get here, so it is a camp for the end of a day, not a place to scout from.
A sandy camp below the riffle, named for the moonshiner Oakie Grogg. Nobody's first choice.
camps.lowNote: The carry from the boats is difficult when the river is low.

camps.d: A large-group camp on a treed bench. There is a small beach, but the easy landing is on the rocky shoreline beside it. The name comes from a steamboat boiler that washed down from a wreck in Big Mallard.
A small low-water camp tucked among large boulders.
A small low-water beach on the left near Campbell's Ferry. The camp is the beach downstream of the rock outcrop, not the bar above it, which is the one people usually pull into by mistake.

A mix of sand and cobble just below the Jim Moore Place, a prospector's homestead with a cluster of buildings he put up himself. Other parties stop here to walk up to the cabins, so expect to share the beach during the day.
One of two 10-person reservable camps, and the only one that keeps its capacity at high water. A good request for a small private trip that wants a guaranteed site in this stretch.
A large camp at Whiplash Rapid. The eddy is on the right, in front of the big rock that gives the rapid its teeth, and it is easy to wash past.
camps.highNote: The Forest Service lists 30 at high water, but Whiplash becomes a very large rapid at high flows and at least one guide calls the camp unreachable then. Scout before you count on it.
camps.conflict: The Forest Service lists a high-water capacity of 30. GoRafting says the camp is not accessible at high flows.

camps.d: A sandy camp just below a pretty creek, with the river trail close by.
A rocky landing with no eddy, then a short carry to a grassy bench where you camp in the field between the buildings. Not often used.
A large, exposed beach just below a rapid and just above Rhett Creek. Plenty of room and very little shade.
A small sand beach at the foot of a cliff with an easy landing and access to the trail.
A low-water sand beach that changes a lot from one year to the next. Have a backup.
A small sloped beach, part sand and part rock, with an easy landing and no shade. Little used.
A small reservable sand beach. The grave marker in camp is for Jack Ranger, who drowned crossing the river here in 1928.
A small beach under a cliff with an easy cobble landing and a grassy, shaded spot to camp. Buckskin Bill's, the Five Mile Bar homestead with a small museum and store, is a walk from here.
camps.conflict: GoRafting places this camp on river right. The Forest Service list, followed here, has it on the left.

camps.d: A pretty camp on a high bench above a small beach, with some shade at the top. The second Pebble Beach on the river, and the larger one.
camps.lowNote: The beach is steep when the river is low.

camps.d: A large camp with a tricky, rocky approach. Aim for the big boulder sitting at the water's edge. The tent sites are on the bar just upstream of it.
A large beach with an easy landing and a long, narrow, grassy flat shaded by pines. Pull in before the river bends and the current picks up. One of the best first-come camps for a big group.
A steep bench beside the Wilson Bar airstrip, the one public airstrip in the river corridor. Also called Jackson Bar. Expect planes, and a climb.
A sunny sand beach by the Mackay Bar pack bridge. A road reaches the river here, and trucks are often parked nearby, so it is the least wild of the reservable camps.
A camp near the Mackay Bar Ranch airstrip. The Forest Service sums it up in three words: air traffic overhead.

The only camp on the list that exists at high water and not at low. It sits at the mouth of the South Fork of the Salmon, technically on the South Fork itself, and it is hard to get into at any level.
camps.lowNote: The Forest Service calls it impossible at low water.
camps.highNote: A high-water option for a full-size group, if you can make the landing.

camps.d: A small, sunny beach at the bottom of the island below the South Fork confluence. The eddy comes up fast as you round the corner.
A small sand beach against a cliff with an easy landing.
camps.conflict: GoRafting places this camp on river left. The Forest Service list, followed here, has it on the right.

camps.d: A small camp at the top of a steep sand beach, named for Henry "Red" Harlan, a longtime river hermit.
camps.lowNote: A cobble beach at the upper end opens up more room.

camps.d: A small camp perched at the top of a steep, sloped sand beach.
Much like its upstream twin: a small camp at the top of a steep sand beach, with room for a few more people.
camps.conflict: GoRafting places this camp on river right. The Forest Service list, followed here, has it on the left.

camps.d: A sloping sand beach with more room than most small camps and a few pines at the upper end for shade.
A large reservable camp. The Forest Service's one piece of advice is to approach the beach from below.
A large reservable camp at Warren Creek with a rocky approach and hiking out of camp. Good at any level.
A sand beach with a grassy flat behind it, also known as Warren Bar. With Mann Creek and Warren Creek it makes three large reservable camps inside a single mile.
A nice camp just below the creek, with a sand beach and an upper bench. A shady trail heads up Indian Creek toward the ranch.
A nice sand beach with a little shade, and a flat grassy field with trees to camp in. Low water only, but big when it is there.
A large low-water sand beach, and the last reservable camp above the Polly Bemis Ranch, the national historic site a short way downstream on the same bank.
A nice beach camp flanked by a few big ponderosas. The Forest Service caps it at 10 people.
A steep sand beach with no shade. Hot in the afternoon.
A small low-water sand beach. Neither source says more about it than that.
A large low-water sand beach above Bull Creek. A hot camp: plan the kitchen around the afternoon sun.

A nice sloping sand beach with a short carry to a flat bench, and a freshwater spring with a small sitting pool. Good hiking upstream toward Upper Bull. Poison ivy grows near the creek. A strong first-come choice for a big group, and it works at any level.
A large, popular camp on a sprawling beach just below California Creek.
camps.highNote: Shrinks from 30 people to 10 at high water.

camps.d: A moderate low-water beach just below California Creek, on the opposite bank.
A very large beach with little or no shade. The camp to ask for with kids along: there is a big sand dune to jump off into the river.
A steep, medium-sized beach with more room on the flat bench above. The eddy is below a jumble of boulders. No afternoon shade.
A beach camp upstream of Sheep Creek with an easy landing on cobble.
A beach of mixed rock and sand just below Sheep Creek that gets late-afternoon shade, which is rare this far down the canyon.
A small beach with a carry up the slope and some shade.

The last reservable camp on the river, a steep sand beach two miles above Long Tom Bar, good for 20 people at any level. A sensible last night if you want a short float to the Vinegar Creek or Carey Creek ramp in the morning.
